copy.headline: Government sets aside 680 million kroner for a new dementia plan

extended.text: The government will set aside 680 million kroner over four years for a new dementia plan in its draft budget for next year. Pia Olsen Dyhr, the economy and interior minister, says there is no concrete plan yet; the money comes first.

She expects the plan to look at giving more people with dementia a permanent coordinator and at training care staff. More than 100,000 Danes over 65 have a dementia diagnosis, and about 400,000 are relatives of someone with the disease. The previous action plan ran out in 2025.

Mette Raun Fjordside, director of Alzheimerforeningen, a patient association, is 'very disappointed' that temporary money is once again going to 'a chronic, fatal brain disease'. She wants dementia to get its own package as a chronic disease.

Christoffer Melson, health spokesperson for Venstre, a liberal party, called the sum 'not immediately impressive'. Venstre had proposed 250 million kroner in 2027 and 500 million a year after that, permanently.

copy.headline: Brazil's president trails his predecessor's son and faces a run-off

standard.text: Flávio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator for the state of Rio de Janeiro, won the first round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday with 47.1 per cent of the vote. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the left-wing president, took 45.1 per cent. As neither won more than 50 per cent, the two meet in a run-off on 25 October.

Lula, 80, called the result 'unexpected'; he had been convinced he would win in the first round. Bolsonaro, 45, is the son of Jair Bolsonaro, the former president Lula beat four years ago. His father is serving 27 years in prison for a failed coup attempt after the 2022 election.

short.text: Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, won the first round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday with 47.1 per cent, ahead of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the president, on 45.1 per cent. The two meet in a run-off on 25 October.

copy.headline: More than one in four Danish pupils are now taught outside public schools

standard.text: More than one in four Danish pupils are now taught outside the folkeskole, Denmark's public primary and lower secondary school. Nearly 20 years ago it was about one in five.
On Bornholm, a Danish island in the Baltic Sea, and in several municipalities in South and West Zealand, the share is more than four in ten.

The figures come from a report by AE, an economic think tank linked to the labour movement. Its chief analyst, Troels Lund Jensen, says the main reason is that parents see quality falling. From next year the government will spend 500 million kroner to prevent school closures.

short.text: More than one in four Danish pupils are now taught outside the folkeskole, Denmark's public primary and lower secondary school, up from about one in five nearly 20 years ago. On Bornholm, a Danish island in the Baltic Sea, it is more than four in ten.

copy.deck: On Bornholm it is more than four in ten; the government has set aside 500 million kroner against school closures.

copy.headline: France suspends lessons at up to 500 high schools after student protests

standard.text: Lessons will be fully or partly suspended at 400 to 500 French high schools on Monday because security conditions 'have not been fulfilled', Édouard Geffray, the education minister, said on Sunday. Twenty-four schools have been burnt or ransacked; 78 staff and about 170 pupils have been injured.
The protests began at a Paris school on 17 September, over teacher absence, long school days and worn-out buildings. More than 5,000 people, most of them minors, have since been arrested.
Gérald Darmanin, the justice minister, has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable, saying they should 'pay for the repairs'.

copy.deck: More than 5,000 people, most of them minors, have been arrested since the protests began.

copy.headline: Russian drone hits Kyiv bridge as Germany's chancellor visits

standard.text: A Russian drone hit Kyiv's Northern Bridge on Sunday, shortly after Friedrich Merz, Germany's chancellor, arrived on an unannounced visit. Two people were injured, said Vitali Klitschko, the city's mayor. It was the fourth day in a row that Russia had targeted the bridges between Kyiv's two banks.

Merz pledged 1 billion euros in military aid and 350 million euros for repairs to Ukraine's energy sector. Executives travelling with him signed 14 agreements worth about 6.6 billion euros, German officials said.
'If Russia is not stopped, the country's war machine will sooner or later turn against us,' Merz said.
